The last column lists what behaves differently — usually the part that costs SolidWorks users an afternoon. Search The five big differences. (1) Creo sketches are always fully defined — weak dimensions fill the gaps. (2) Creo saves numbered versions and keeps models in session memory: set the working directory, erase what you don't need. (3) Names are unique in session; assemblies find parts by name. (4) Datum planes and axes are central — build on them. (5) Regeneration failures stop you until you resolve them; fragile references cost more in Creo. Resolving Viscous Forces in CFD 22 Jun 2018 1 min read Education What is the method used by FLUENT to evaluate the viscous forces (breakdown) on wall BC? Answer 1 If you are simulating a flat plate at zero angle of attack then all the viscous forces will be along X(streamwise direction) and all the pressure forces along Y (normal to wall). But for an aerofoil, there is a local slope for the wall at every point so in the global coordinates the shear forces will have x and y components. At every local point along the wall the shear force will be tangential to it and pressure forces normal to it. Since the aerofoil, generally. has a curvature with varying slopes there will always be x and y components for both shear and pressure forces. Are you a gaslighter? 29 Oct 2023 1 min read Relationship What is gas lighting? Gaslighting is a form of psychological manipulation in which a person or a group of people subtly or overtly manipulates someone else's perception of reality. The term "gaslighting" originated from a play called "Gas Light" and later a movie adaptation, both of which portrayed a husband who manipulated his wife into believing she was going insane by dimming the gas lights in their home. In the context of psychological manipulation, gaslighting typically involves tactics such as: Denial: The gaslighter may deny certain events or experiences, making the victim doubt their own memory or perception of reality. Discrediting: Gaslighters may undermine the victim's credibility or make them doubt their own abilities, making them feel inadequate or incapable. We stake claims, defend what’s "ours," and sometimes destroy what was someone else’s, all in the name of progress or protection. It is pure, powerful, and rare. It is the kind of love that says, "I love you, no matter what." What is Unconditional Love? Unconditional love means loving someone without expecting anything in return . It is not dependent on the other person’s actions, behavior, success, or appearance. It is acceptance in its truest form , where the flaws, mistakes, and imperfections are all embraced. Unlike most relationships where love is given based on conditions— "If you do this, I’ll love you," or "I love you because you are successful/kind/beautiful" —unconditional love needs no reason and has no limits .

The path seemed endless to my little feet, but the sights around me filled me with wonder. We passed through coconut groves, mango orchards, and even small honey-bee farms . The patient needs rest, and the caretaker already has enough on their shoulders — so why add another visitor, another conversation, another ripple in an already tense atmosphere? But as life unfolded, I began to see things differently. A hospital visit, I realized, is not an act of disturbance — it’s an act of humanity. It’s not about bringing words; it’s about bringing presence. When you walk into that quiet, antiseptic room with a smile, you’re not there to heal the illness, but to heal the spirit that’s fighting it. My grandfather lived a simple life — a plate of wholesome food, a roof over his head, and a peaceful community around him. My father needed a little more — proper schooling for his children, a bicycle or a transistor to stay connected. Today, I have many needs — a car, a smartphone, conveniences that I consider essentials. And my son? He dreams of gadgets that didn’t even exist a decade ago. We often forget that the most fundamental needs of human beings are still just food, shelter, and meaningful connection . Everything beyond that gradually shifts from “need” to “want,” yet society convinces us that every want is a necessity. We spend a considerable part of our lives trying to become capable. We study to earn a living. We work to support a family. We save to feel secure. We gather knowledge, develop skills, and slowly find our place in the world. Along this journey, we often ask: What more do I need to be happy? Then, sometimes through a very ordinary experience, another question appears: What do I already have that could make someone else’s life a little better? That question can change the way we experience our own lives. Perhaps we help a student understand something that has troubled them for weeks. Everyone Loves a Ship That Sails Smoothly When a ship sails smoothly across the ocean, there is no shortage of passengers. Everyone enjoys the journey, admires the captain, appreciates the comfort, and proudly associates themselves with its success. But when the ship begins to sink, something interesting happens. The very same passengers who once celebrated the voyage begin looking for lifeboats. Some leave immediately. Some hesitate. Some wait until the situation becomes unbearable. You play against Arun (left), Meena (top) and Ravi (right). One 52-card deck is dealt out, 13 cards each. Play goes clockwise: You → Arun → Meena → Ravi. First player to get rid of all their cards wins. A round The player who starts a round places 1 to 4 cards face down on the pile and names any rank, e.g. "three 7s". The number of cards is always visible; only the rank may be a lie. Each following player must either place 1–4 cards claiming the same rank , or pass . After any play, anyone may shout "Bluff!" . The cards just played are turned over: If any of them is not of the claimed rank, the liar picks up the whole pile. If they are all genuine, the caller picks up the whole pile. How to play FreeCell All 52 cards are dealt face up into 8 columns. Goal: move every card to the 4 foundations (top right), building up by suit from Ace to King. Columns : build down in alternating colours (red 6 on black 7). Any card may go into an empty column. Free cells (top left): each holds one card. Officially only one card moves at a time; moving a run is a shortcut ("supermove") for several single moves through free cells and empty columns. The longest run you can move is (free cells + 1) × 2^(empty columns) , halved when the destination is itself an empty column. content: High Efficiency · No Axial Thrust · Easy to Manufacture · Higher Noise · Parallel Shafts Only · Proven Reliability · Pressure Angle Effect · Standard Mounting Configurations · Curvature Sum — The Key Stress Driver · 1 · Tangential Load · 2 · Bending Stress (AGMA 2101) · 3 · Contact (Hertzian) Stress (AGMA 2101) · 4 · AGMA Safety Factors · 5 · Key Material Properties (Carburised Steel) · 6 · Shaft Offset Effects on Stress · Geometry · Forces & Stress Indicators · Failure Diagnosis Matrix · Scheduled Maintenance Programme · Condition Monitoring Parameters · Lubrication Guide Spur Gear Fundamentals The simplest and most common cylindrical gear — straight teeth cut parallel to the rotation axis, transmitting power between parallel shafts. Spur gears are the baseline of mechanical power transmission. Their teeth are cut straight across the face, generating only radial (tangential + radial) loads — no axial thrust, which simplifies shaft and bearing design. The involute tooth profile, universal since the 18th century, ensures constant velocity ratio under load and is tolerant of small centre-distance errors. Operating characteristics are dominated by two competing stress regimes: bending stress at the tooth root (Lewis/AGMA) and Hertzian contact stress at the flank (surface fatigue). Gear design is the art of balancing these with material selection, tooth geometry, and lubrication. ⚡ High Efficiency 98–99.5% efficiency per mesh under full load with adequate lubr

There are two legitimate answers, and confusing them is the single most common error in balancing work. The kinematic velocity — how fast the mass centre travels around the rotational axis. This follows from U , m and N alone, needs no other information, and is the ISO 1940 balance quality grade G . The response velocity — what a transducer actually measures on the machine. This is the kinematic value multiplied by a dynamic amplification factor that depends on the structure: natural frequency, damping, and where you put the probe. The first is a property of the rotor. title: What's Inside Spills Out
snippet: Zen Series, Story 1 — a monk, a bump, and a cup of tea.
content: Zen Series, Story 1 — a monk, a bump, and a cup of tea. What's Inside Spills Out · The Story · Reflection Zen Series Story 01 What's Inside Spills Out Small stories, still minds. A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story A monk was walking along, holding a cup of tea. Someone hurrying past, not watching where they were going, knocked into him — and the tea splashed out onto the ground. A student standing nearby remarked, “Look, you've spilled your tea.” The monk smiled and said: “Had it been coffee in the cup, only coffee would have spilled.” Reflection The lesson is quietly piercing. When life bumps into us — and it always will — what pours out is simply whatever we were already carrying inside. The jolt doesn't create anything. It only reveals what was there all along. title: Maybe
snippet: Zen Series, Story 3 — An old farmer, a runaway horse, and a word that keeps the story open.
content: Zen Series, Story 3 — An old farmer, a runaway horse, and a word that keeps the story open. Maybe · The Story · Reflection Zen Series Story 03 Maybe Small stories, still minds. A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story An old farmer had worked his fields for many years. One day his only horse broke through the fence and ran off into the hills. The neighbours came round. “What terrible luck,” they said. “Maybe,” said the farmer. Next morning the horse came back, bringing three wild horses with it. “How wonderful!” said the neighbours. “Maybe,” said the farmer. The day after, his son tried to ride one of the wild horses, was thrown, and broke his leg. “Such misfortune,” said the neighbours. “Maybe,” said the farmer. A week later, officers came through the village taking every young man for the army. They looked at the son’s leg and passed him by. “You are so lucky,” said the neighbours. “Maybe,” said the farmer. title: Is That So?
snippet: Zen Series, Story 4 — Blame, praise, a baby left at a hermit’s door, and three quiet words.
content: Zen Series, Story 4 — Blame, praise, a baby left at a hermit’s door, and three quiet words. Is That So? · The Story · Reflection Zen Series Story 04 Is That So? Small stories, still minds. A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story The Zen master Hakuin was respected in his village as a man of pure life. Nearby lived a family with a young daughter. One day her parents discovered she was expecting a child. Angry and ashamed, they demanded to know the father’s name. Frightened, she named Hakuin. The parents stormed to his hut and poured out their accusations. Hakuin listened, and said only: “Is that so?” When the child was born, they brought the baby to him. “He is yours. You raise him.” His good name was gone, but Hakuin took the baby in and cared for him tenderly, begging milk and food from neighbours who now looked down on him. A year passed. The young mother could bear it no longer and told her parents the truth: the father was a young man who worked at the fish market.

Then the teacher said: “We cannot always avoid the first arrow. The second one we shoot ourselves.” Reflection The first arrow is the event: the remark, the loss, the illness, the delay. Tea ran over the rim, across the saucer and onto the floor. The professor watched until he could restrain himself no longer. “It is overfull! No more will go in!” Nan-in set down the pot. “Like this cup, you are full of your own opinions. How can I show you Zen unless you first empty your cup?” Reflection In Story 01 the cup spilled what was already inside it; this one cannot take in anything new. At the edge of a cliff he caught hold of a wild vine and swung himself over the side. Hanging there, he looked up: the tiger was pacing at the top, sniffing at him. He looked down: far below, a second tiger was waiting for him to fall. Then two mice, one black and one white, crept out and began to gnaw, little by little, at the vine he was holding. Just then the man noticed a wild strawberry growing from the cliff face beside him. Holding the vine with one hand, he reached out with the other and picked it. How sweet it tasted! Just then he heard his teacher’s footsteps approaching, so he quickly hid the pieces behind his back. When the master came in, Ikkyu asked him in his most serious voice, “Teacher, why do people have to die?” “It is natural,” said the master. “Everything that comes into being must one day pass away. A quiet young man who was passing stopped to listen. He was Hui-neng, who would one day become the Sixth Patriarch of Zen. At last he spoke: “It is not the wind that is moving, and not the flag. It is your minds that are moving.” Reflection The two monks were each half right, and both completely caught. The flag kept flapping and the wind kept blowing whatever they decided. He had done it only minutes earlier, but without noticing. He realised he had not yet learned to carry his Zen into every minute. He became Nan-in’s pupil and trained for six more years. The next day he did not eat either, nor the day after that. “He must be upset that we hid his tools,” the students whispered. “We had better put them back.” So they did. That day the old master worked in the garden as usual, and that evening he ate his meal. Hogen joined them and pointed to a large stone lying nearby. “Tell me,” he said, “is this stone inside your mind, or outside it?” One monk answered confidently: “From the Buddhist point of view, everything is an expression of mind. He travelled the country for ten years collecting money — much of it in tiny coins from people who had little to give — and he thanked every giver with the same gratitude. At last he had enough. Just then the river flooded and famine followed. Tetsugen took everything he had raised and spent it feeding the hungry. Then he began collecting again. A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story A monk who had just arrived at the monastery went to the master Joshu and said, “I have only just entered this place. Then the sigh of the wind. Then the hoot of an owl. Then the hum of insects. Each time the answer was no. For almost a year he came with sound after sound, and every one was rejected. A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story Two monks were washing their bowls in a river when they saw a scorpion that had fallen in and was drowning. One monk scooped it out at once and set it on the bank — and as he did, it stung him. He went back to washing his bowl. A little later the scorpion fell into the water again. Again the monk lifted it out, and again it stung him. His companion could not bear to watch any more. “Why do you keep saving it? You know it will sting you every time.” “It is the scorpion’s nature to sting,” said the monk. “It is my nature to save. Why should I give up my nature because of its nature?” Reflection This old tale, told in many traditions, is about who decides how we behave. The scorpion is simply being a scorpion. snippet: Zen Series, Story 28 — An angry man pours insults on a teacher. The teacher asks about gifts.
content: Zen Series, Story 28 — An angry man pours insults on a teacher. The teacher asks about gifts. The Gift Not Taken · The Story · Reflection Zen Series Story 28 The Gift Not Taken Small stories, still minds. A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story A man who disliked the Buddha came to find him and, in front of everyone, poured out insult after insult. The Buddha listened quietly until the man ran out of words. Then he asked, “If someone offers you a gift and you do not accept it, to whom does the gift belong?” “To the one who offered it, of course,” said the man. The Buddha nodded. “Then I do not accept your abuse. You may keep it.” Reflection This story, much loved in Zen as in all of Buddhism, makes a simple point with great force: an insult only lands if we pick it up. The angry man did all the giving; the Buddha simply declined to receive. A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story The Buddha was travelling with his attendant Ananda. Feeling thirsty, he asked Ananda to fetch some water from a stream they had just passed. When Ananda reached the stream, a bullock cart had just crossed it. The water was churned up and brown with mud. He came back and said, “The water is too dirty to drink.” After a while the Buddha asked him to go again. The water was still a little cloudy, and Ananda returned once more. Some time later, the Buddha sent him a third time. Now the mud had sunk to the bottom, and the water was clear and fresh. Ananda brought some back. The Buddha looked at it and said: “See — you did nothing to the water. You only let it be, and it became clear by itself. Your mind is the same.” Reflection When we are up

A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story A blind man had spent the evening visiting a friend. When it was time to leave, the friend offered him a lantern for the walk home. “I have no need of a lantern,” said the blind man, laughing. “Light and darkness are the same to me.” “I know,” said his friend. “But if you carry it, others will see you and won’t bump into you.” So the blind man set off with the lantern. He had not gone far when someone walked straight into him. “Watch where you are going!” he cried. “Can’t you see my lantern?” “Brother,” said the stranger, “your candle has gone out.” Reflection The blind man had done the sensible thing — he took the light. The son swept the path, raked the gravel and washed the stepping stones until everything shone. “Not quite yet,” said Rikyu. The son swept again, more carefully still. “Still not right.” At last the son said, “Father, there is nothing left to do. Every leaf is gone. Every stone is clean.” Rikyu walked into the garden, took hold of a branch of a maple tree, and gave it a gentle shake. A few leaves floated down and settled here and there on the spotless path. “Now,” he said, “it is ready.” Reflection The son had made the garden perfect, and in doing so had made it lifeless. In front of the master, the young man hit the centre of a distant target with his first arrow — and then split that arrow down the middle with his second. “Match that if you can,” he said. The old man said nothing, but beckoned him to follow up into the mountains. They came to a deep gorge crossed by a single shaky log. The master walked calmly out to the middle of it, chose a tree far away, drew his bow and hit it cleanly. “Now it is your turn,” he said, stepping back to the cliff. title: No Merit
snippet: Zen Series, Story 33 — An emperor lists his good works and asks what he has earned. The answer stuns him.
content: Zen Series, Story 33 — An emperor lists his good works and asks what he has earned. The answer stuns him. No Merit · The Story · Reflection Zen Series Story 33 No Merit Small stories, still minds. A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story When the monk Bodhidharma arrived in China from India, Emperor Wu, a devout patron of Buddhism, invited him to the palace. “I have built many temples,” said the emperor. “I have had the scriptures copied and supported thousands of monks and nuns. What merit have I earned?” “No merit at all,” said Bodhidharma. The emperor was taken aback. “Then what is the first principle of the holy teaching?” “Vast emptiness,” said Bodhidharma. “Nothing holy.” “Then who,” asked the emperor, “is this standing in front of me?” “I don’t know,” said Bodhidharma. Reflection The emperor’s good works were real, and they did real good. But he was keeping accounts, as if goodness were a deposit that would pay him back with interest. A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story A monk named Huike had studied for many years, but his mind gave him no rest. He travelled through the winter snow to find the master Bodhidharma, who was meditating in the mountains. “My mind is not at peace,” Huike said. “Please, Master — pacify my mind.” “Very well,” said Bodhidharma. “Bring me your mind, and I will pacify it.” Huike was silent for a long while. He searched and searched. At last he said, “I have looked for my mind everywhere, and I cannot find it.” “There,” said Bodhidharma. “I have pacified it for you.” Reflection Huike came with his restlessness as though it were a solid object that someone could fix. The man took offence and challenged him to a duel the next morning. The tea master had never held a sword in earnest. In despair he went to a fencing teacher. “I know nothing of fighting,” he said. “All I know is the way of tea.” “Then make me some tea,” said the fencing teacher. The tea master forgot his fear and prepared tea, as he always did, with complete calm and attention. The fencing teacher watched closely, then said: “Tomorrow, face your opponent exactly as you are now. Raise your sword with the same calm with which you raised that bowl. content: Zen Series, Story 36 — A man asks a master to write down the highest wisdom. The master writes one word. Attention · The Story · Reflection Zen Series Story 36 Attention Small stories, still minds. A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story A man came to the master Ikkyu and said, “Will you please write down for me some maxims of the highest wisdom?” Ikkyu picked up his brush and wrote one word: Attention. “Is that all?” said the man. “Won’t you add something more?” So Ikkyu wrote again: Attention. Attention. “Well,” said the man, a little annoyed, “I really don’t see much depth in that.” Ikkyu wrote the same word three times: Attention. Attention. Attention. Now the man was irritated. “What does ‘attention’ mean, anyway?” Ikkyu answered gently: “Attention means attention.” Reflection The man was looking for something impressive — a saying he could frame and admire. A wealthy merchant named Umezu decided to give five hundred pieces of gold towards a larger building, and brought the money to the master himself. “All right,” said Seisetsu. “I will take it.” Umezu gave him the sack of gold, but he was not satisfied with the master’s manner. “There are five hundred pieces in that sack,” he said. “You told me so already,” said Seisetsu. “Even for a wealthy merchant, five hundred pieces is a great deal of money,” Umezu went on. “Do you want me to thank you for it?” asked Seisetsu. “You ought to,” said Umezu. “Why should I?” said Seisetsu. “The giver should be the one who is thankful.” Reflection Umezu’s gift was generous, but he wa

title: The Flower Sermon
snippet: Zen Series, Story 38 — The Buddha gives a sermon without a single word. Only one listener smiles.
content: Zen Series, Story 38 — The Buddha gives a sermon without a single word. Only one listener smiles. The Flower Sermon · The Story · Reflection Zen Series Story 38 The Flower Sermon Small stories, still minds. A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story Once a great crowd gathered on Vulture Peak to hear the Buddha teach. They waited for him to speak. The Buddha said nothing. He simply held up a single flower and turned it gently in his fingers. The crowd was puzzled. They looked at one another, wondering what he meant and when the sermon would begin. Only one disciple, Mahakashyapa, looked at the flower — and smiled. The Buddha said: “I have a treasure beyond words, a teaching passed from mind to mind. I give it to Mahakashyapa.” Reflection This is the story Zen tells about its own beginning: a teaching passed not through words but through seeing. content: Zen Series, Story 39 — A man’s boat is bumped on the river. Whether he gets angry depends on what he sees. The Empty Boat · The Story · Reflection Zen Series Story 39 The Empty Boat Small stories, still minds. A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story This old story comes from the Chinese sage Chuang Tzu, and Zen has always loved it. A man was rowing across a river when another boat drifted into his and knocked against it. He turned around, ready to shout — but the other boat was empty. It had simply come loose and floated downstream. His anger vanished; there was no one to be angry with. Now suppose there had been someone sitting in the other boat. He would have shouted at him to steer clear. If that did not work he would shout again, and then curse — all because someone was in the boat. A short Zen tale each time, with a thought to carry into the day. 禅 Read ↓ The Story The Buddha once told this parable to his monks. A man on a long journey came to a great river. The near bank was dangerous and the far bank safe, but there was no bridge and no ferry. So he gathered sticks, grass and branches, bound them into a raft, and paddling with his hands and feet, crossed safely to the other side. Then he thought, “This raft has been so useful to me.
